name: Louis XIV
kicker: France’s “Sun King” · Longest-reigning monarch, built Versailles
briefing: Louis XIV became king of France at only four years old and kept the job for 72 years, still the longest confirmed reign of any monarch in European history. He expanded a royal hunting lodge into the dazzling Palace of Versailles, forced nobles to live there so he could watch them, and liked being called the “Sun King” because, like the sun, he believed everything in France revolved around him. He may never have actually said “I am the state,” but it sure sounds like him.
answerHtml: Louis XIV (or Louis the Great; prompt on Louis or Sun King)

clues.t: Nicknamed the “Sun King” because he believed France revolved around him, the way planets circle the sun
Expanded a royal hunting lodge into the enormous Palace of Versailles and moved his whole court there
Became king at only four years old in 1643, when his father (the previous king) died
Reigned for 72 years, from 1643 to 1715, the longest confirmed reign of any monarch in European history
Required many French nobles to spend part of the year living at Versailles, where he could watch them closely
Survived a series of noble and parliamentary revolts against royal power in his childhood, known as the Fronde [“frond”]
During his childhood, Cardinal Mazarin [“MA-zuh-ran”] ran the government for him as chief minister
Issued the 1685 Edict of Fontainebleau [“fon-TEN-bloh”], revoking the Edict of Nantes and driving out many Huguenot Protestants
Is remembered for the proud, probably made-up, quote “I am the state”
Tried to put his grandson Philip of Anjou on the throne of Spain, starting the War of the Spanish Succession
Finance minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert [“kohl-BEAR”] built up French trade, manufacturing, and the navy
Married his cousin Maria Theresa of Spain in 1660 as part of a peace treaty between France and Spain
His War of Devolution was cut short by the Triple Alliance; his later Dutch War ended with the Treaty of Nijmegen [“NY-may-khen”]
Later fought the War of the League of Augsburg, which ended with the 1697 Treaty of Ryswick [“RIZ-wick”]
Used the dragonnades [“drag-oh-NAHDS”], billeting soldiers in Protestant homes, to pressure Huguenots into converting
Sent hundreds of unmarried women nicknamed the “king’s daughters” to help populate France’s colony in Canada
Began ruling personally in 1661 after Mazarin’s death and never again appointed a chief minister
Belonged to the Bourbon [“BOOR-bon”] dynasty, which had ruled France since his grandfather Henry IV
His military engineer, the Marquis de Vauban [“voh-BAHN”], ringed France’s borders with star-shaped forts
Supported playwright Molière [“mohl-YAIR”] and composer Jean-Baptiste Lully [“loo-LEE”] at his court
Had the Hall of Mirrors built at Versailles to display French glassmaking to foreign visitors
Successfully made his grandson the first Bourbon king of Spain, Philip V
Outlived his son and grandson, so his five-year-old great-grandson inherited the throne in 1715

trap.title: Which Louis?
trap.body: Eighteen French kings were named Louis, and quiz bowl loves mixing them up. His father, Louis XIII, ruled during the Thirty Years’ War and relied on Cardinal Richelieu — not Mazarin, and not Versailles. A much later descendant, Louis XVI, was guillotined in the French Revolution, as was his wife, Marie Antoinette. Saying just “Louis” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Versailles, the Sun King, the Fronde, Cardinal Mazarin, and a 72-year reign mean Louis XIV. Richelieu and the Thirty Years’ War mean Louis XIII; the guillotine and Marie Antoinette mean Louis XVI. Always say the number.
